title: Solomon Secures the Throne
overview: As David dies, Solomon becomes king and removes, one by one, the men seen as threats to his rule.

parts.label: David's last advice (vv. 1-4)
parts.note: Near death, David urges Solomon to be strong and to keep the law God gave through Moses. He ties this to God's earlier promise that David's family would keep the throne if they stayed faithful.

parts.label: Old scores to settle (vv. 5-9)
parts.note: David names Joab, his army chief, who murdered two rival commanders in peacetime, and Shimei, who cursed David during Absalom's revolt and whom David had sworn not to kill. He asks Solomon to make sure neither dies in peace, but to honor the family of Barzillai, who stood by David when he fled.

parts.label: David dies (vv. 10-12)
parts.note: David is buried in Jerusalem after a reign of forty years. Solomon takes his place, and his rule is firmly in place.

parts.label: Adonijah's fatal request (vv. 13-25)
parts.note: Adonijah, the older brother who had tried to take the throne, asks Bathsheba, now honored as queen mother, to help him marry Abishag, the young woman who had cared for the dying David. In that world, taking a late king's woman could signal a claim to his crown, so Solomon treats it as a new bid for power and has Adonijah killed.

parts.label: Abiathar banished, Joab killed (vv. 26-35)
parts.note: Abiathar the priest, who had backed Adonijah, is spared for his years of loyalty to David but sent home, which the writer sees as fulfilling an old warning against the priestly family of Eli. Joab grabs the horns of the altar, its raised corners where people sought sanctuary, but the law gave no refuge to deliberate murderers, and Solomon has him struck down there.

parts.label: Shimei's broken terms (vv. 36-46)
parts.note: Solomon confines Shimei to Jerusalem on pain of death, and when Shimei leaves three years later to fetch runaway slaves from the Philistine city of Gath, Solomon has him executed. The chapter closes with the line that the kingdom was now firmly in Solomon's hands.

disagreement: Readers differ over whether the writer presents these deaths as just punishment that secured the throne God promised, or quietly exposes the ruthless politics behind Solomon's rise, including David's way around his own oath to Shimei.
think: Can someone keep the exact words of a promise while breaking its spirit, and where would you draw that line?
